name: Hydrogen peroxide rinse DIY
lead: A hydrogen peroxide rinse is a do-it-yourself practice in which diluted household hydrogen peroxide, commonly the 3 percent pharmacy solution, is swished in the mouth to get whiter-looking teeth and a fresher mouth. It draws on the fact that hydrogen peroxide, directly or as carbamide peroxide, is the main active ingredient in tooth whitening, and a brighter smile is a common aim in appearance forums.[1][2]

Whitening peroxide works as an oxidiser: Wikipedia explains that it releases free radicals that break pigment molecules into smaller, less coloured pieces, so teeth reflect more light and look whiter.[1] In-office treatment may lighten teeth by 2 to 7 shades, strips and trays by about 1 to 2 shades, and whitening rinses may take up to three months to show results.[1]

Dilute peroxide rinses have been reviewed for gingivitis and plaque, where they did better than placebo, though chlorhexidine was judged much more effective.[2] Regulators treat consumer strengths differently: the EU limits retail hydrogen peroxide to 0.1 percent, with 0.1 to 6 percent allowed only through dental professionals for adults, and the US FDA endorses gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide.[1]

chain: Oxidises coloured molecules in tooth structure
angle.text: People swish diluted peroxide hoping to lighten surface stains and brighten their smile the way professional peroxide gels do. Commercial products control concentration and contact time, which a home rinse does not.

infobox: Under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide [1]

paras: Consumer hydrogen peroxide solutions are usually 3 or 6 percent by weight and sold through pharmacies, mainly for cleaning and disinfecting.[2] Online discussions describe swishing a diluted portion of the 3 percent solution and spitting it out. Dilution and timing instructions are not given here.

Carbamide peroxide breaks down in water to release hydrogen peroxide, which diffuses into the tooth and oxidises pigment molecules.[1] In-office gels typically contain 10 to 44 percent carbamide peroxide, roughly 3 to 16 percent hydrogen peroxide, and power-bleaching gels can reach 25 to 38 percent.[1] Rebound is common: nearly half of the change from an intensive one-hour session may be lost within seven days as teeth rehydrate.[1]

Studies of whitening cover gels, strips and trays with defined concentrations; Wikipedia's tooth whitening article says rinses can take up to three months to show results.[1] As a mouth rinse for gum health, reviews cited on Wikipedia found dilute peroxide better than placebo but far less effective than chlorhexidine.[2]

Hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or higher can damage tissue and irritate mucous membranes, and sensitivity affects 67 to 78 percent of people receiving in-office hydrogen peroxide treatment with heat, lasting about 4 to 39 days.[1] Home bleaching that follows manufacturer instructions causes less sensitivity than in-office bleaching.[1]

Wikipedia notes that concentrations as low as 3 percent can be dangerous for the eye.[2] Carbamide peroxide can increase enamel roughness and porosity, and the long-term effects of concentrations above 6 percent are not clarified.[1]
No studies found of the home-made rinse for whitening specifically. Related research on peroxide whitening gels and peroxide mouthrinses for gingivitis is summarised above.[1][2]

In the EU only dental professionals may provide products with 0.1 to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide, and only to patients aged 18 or older.[1] In 2010 the UK General Dental Council raised concerns about poor-quality whitening by untrained staff.[1]

timeline.event: UK General Dental Council raises concerns about whitening by untrained staff.[1]

card.summary: Swishing diluted household hydrogen peroxide for whiter teeth, with irritation concerns and thin direct evidence.
card.note: Regulators limit consumer peroxide strengths; mucous membrane irritation is documented at higher concentrations.

quick.overview:
The do-it-yourself hydrogen peroxide rinse involves swishing diluted household peroxide, typically the 3 percent pharmacy solution, in the mouth in the hope of whitening teeth and freshening the mouth. It borrows from the fact that peroxide is the main active ingredient in professional and commercial whitening products.

Those products use controlled gels in measured concentrations and contact times. Little published research has tested the home rinse itself.
quick.mechanism: Hydrogen peroxide, directly or released from carbamide peroxide, oxidises coloured molecules in tooth structure. Commercial products control concentration, delivery and contact time; a DIY rinse does not.
quick.risks: Sources describe peroxide at 10 percent or more as capable of damaging tissue and burning mucous membranes, and tooth sensitivity is common with whitening. Regulators set limits on consumer products, for example 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide in the EU, and 3 percent solutions are noted as hazardous to the eye.
